hero.title: Image-In Web Application
paragraphs: Image-In is a lightweight web application built to make image analysis feel simple and developer-friendly. Users can drag and drop an image and receive a clean JSON response containing detected data, without needing to deal with complex setup or external tools. The goal was to keep the experience minimal and approachable while still delivering structured, machine-readable output.

I built Image-In as both a technical experiment and a design exercise, focusing on how to hide complexity behind an intuitive interface. The frontend uses React with Next.js and Tailwind CSS, while the backend handles image processing and structured response generation. A key focus of the project was keeping frontend interactions and backend logic tightly aligned to create a fast, predictable, and reliable user experience.

concepts.label: KEY CONCEPTS LEARNED
items: Drag-and-drop UX requires careful event and state handling.
API latency directly affects perceived app quality.
Frontend–backend contracts need to be defined early.
Error handling is as important as the happy path.
File uploads expose edge cases in validation and security.
Clear loading states improve usability and trust.
Simple APIs are easier to evolve than complex ones.

body.title: Product Idea & Problem Framing
paragraphs: Image-In started as an exploration into how image analysis and machine learning could be exposed through a simple, accessible web interface. The core idea was to allow users to drag and drop an image and receive structured insights without needing to understand anything about how the analysis worked behind the scenes. My goal was to design a workflow that felt instant and frictionless. From the moment a user landed on the page, it needed to be obvious what the product did and how to use it. This led to a highly minimal interface with a single primary interaction: upload an image and view the generated output. The simplicity of the UI was deliberate, allowing the technical complexity of the backend to remain invisible to the user.

body.title: System Architecture & API Design
paragraphs: The application was built around a clear client–server separation. The frontend, developed with Next.js and React, handled user interaction, file uploads, and result presentation. The backend, written in C#, exposed a REST API responsible for receiving image data, running analysis pipelines, and returning structured JSON responses.

Designing the API forced me to think carefully about data contracts, error handling, and request lifecycles. Each endpoint was built to be stateless and predictable, making the system easier to test and reason about. This project significantly deepened my understanding of how frontend and backend concerns intersect and how thoughtful API design can simplify both sides of an application.

body.title: Iteration, UX Refinement, and Reliability
paragraphs: Early versions of Image-In exposed too much technical detail to the user and required unnecessary steps to complete a single upload. Through iterative testing and self-critique, I simplified the flow down to its essentials and focused on making the upload-to-result transition feel smooth and immediate.

I also invested time into improving reliability and user feedback, adding loading states, basic validation, and clearer error messages. These refinements reinforced how much perceived quality depends on small UX details. The final result is a compact but expressive product that demonstrates how a complex technical system can be packaged into a simple, approachable user experience.
